question.worked_solution:
First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{11\pi }{2}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{11\pi }{2}-2\pi  & =\frac{7\pi }{2} \\ \frac{7\pi }{2}-2\pi  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}).$

The angle $(\frac{3\pi }{2})$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253609/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $(\frac{3\pi }{2})$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{2})=-1.$
